nameStory: This little buttercup gets its name from its love of water — 'water-crowfoot' refers to the way its divided leaves resemble a crow's foot print when pressed flat. The 'small yellow' part distinguishes it from its larger cousin, the yellow water-crowfoot, as this species has more modest blooms that rarely exceed half an inch across.
description: Small yellow water-crowfoot is a low-growing perennial that lives both in shallow water and on muddy shores. It spreads along the ground or floats just beneath the water surface, sending up small bright yellow flowers that look like tiny buttercups. The plant rarely stands more than a few inches tall, instead creating mats of rounded, deeply-divided leaves that feel soft and somewhat succulent to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow buttercup-like flowers with 5 glossy petals, each bloom less than half an inch across with a slightly waxy feel when touched gently

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round or kidney-shaped leaves divided into 3 main parts that may be further subdivided, feeling somewhat thick and fleshy compared to typical buttercup leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Prostrate stems that either creep along muddy ground or float in shallow water, never standing upright but spreading horizontally

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Stems and leaves can be either smooth and hairless or covered with fine soft hairs, giving some plants a slightly fuzzy feel

habitat: Look for this rare plant along the muddy edges of ponds, slow streams, and marshes, especially in northern New England's cooler regions. It thrives in shallow water or on wet shores where the soil stays consistently moist, often growing alongside sedges and other wetland plants in areas that flood seasonally.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as the water warms, with the distinctive three-parted foliage appearing first along shorelines and in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the small yellow flowers are most visible, floating just above the water surface or nestled among the leaves on muddy shores.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to die back, though some foliage may persist in milder areas until frost arrives.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts, surviving as roots and underground stems in the mud.

funFact: This little buttercup is so rare in Maine that it's protected by state law — with only 4 recorded sightings in all of New England, you're more likely to spot a moose than find this elusive aquatic wildflower!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its larger relative, yellow water-crowfoot, but small yellow water-crowfoot has noticeably smaller flowers (less than half an inch vs. up to an inch across) and more rounded, kidney-shaped leaves rather than the fan-shaped leaves of its bigger cousin.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name honors Johann Georg Gmelin, an 18th-century German botanist who explored Siberia — fitting since this cold-loving plant spans both northern North America and Eurasia, representing an ancient connection between continents.
compareHints: Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit. It's much smaller than yellow water-crowfoot and lacks the deeply-dissected underwater leaves that many aquatic buttercups develop.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
